title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
Skip to main content
In this class you’ll analyze real CDC survey data (NHANES, August 2021–August 2023) with Claude Code in Positron. Claude Code is an AI coding agent: it reads your files, writes code, runs it, and fixes its own errors. You’ll work in its extension panel. You’ll plan first, let Claude build the scripts, and check every step yourself. By the end, you’ll try to reproduce a published CDC estimate of how many U.S. adults have high blood pressure. This page has every prompt, ready to copy.
The goal: this class doesn’t replace learning R or statistics. You’ll learn where a coding agent speeds up good analysis, and where your expertise must stay in control. Each step below says what Claude does and what you decide.
For: researchers, research coordinators, analysts, and clinicians who can read a little R. Getting started with Claude (the Claude app class) helps but isn’t required. If you work in Python, pair with an R user or follow along.
By the end of class, you’ll be able to:

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
Before class






ImportantSetup (about 30 minutes)



Do the setup steps before class. In short: a Yale Claude account whose seat includes Claude Code, Positron with the Claude Code extension, R with the class packages (including haven and survey), and git with your name and email set.
crumbs: Analyzing research data with Claude Code

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
Download
nhanes-bp.zip is the class project. It holds:

three unmodified CDC data files in data/raw/ (DEMO_L.xpt demographics, BPXO_L.xpt blood pressure readings, BPQ_L.xpt blood pressure questions), with CDC’s codebooks in docs/codebooks/
a data dictionary of the variables we use (data/data_dictionary.csv)
a one-page analysis plan (docs/analysis-plan.md)
CLAUDE.md, the project rules for Claude
a fictional stand-in in data/restricted/
an excerpt of CDC’s own SAS code in legacy/, for a try-at-home exercise

The R/, output/, and reports/ folders are empty. You’ll fill them in class.
Unzip it somewhere easy to find, such as Documents/. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All. If you get an nhanes-bp folder inside another nhanes-bp folder, open the inner one. CLAUDE.md should be at the top of Positron’s Explorer. Then open the nhanes-bp folder in Positron (File → Open Folder).
nhanes-bp-checkpoint.zip is for if you fall behind. It’s the same project with a working R/01_prepare.R. You only need it if your own script isn’t working by the catch-up point.






ImportantData rule for today




The data are real. NHANES is a public, de-identified CDC survey. It isn’t patient data, but the NCHS data user agreement still applies: use the data for statistical analysis only, never try to identify anyone, and never link it to other data about the same people.
data/restricted/ is fictional. It holds one made-up file that stands in for data Claude must never read.
Don’t add PHI or data under a data use agreement to this project. Guardrails like deny rules are safety nets. They don’t make it OK to keep restricted data in a folder Claude Code works in. Policy comes first: follow Yale’s data classification.
A HIPAA-supported version of Claude is available by request (see the ITS service page for Claude Enterprise). It doesn’t approve your project, every feature, or every data set, and its features may differ. Check with ITS before using Claude Code with sensitive data.

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
section: 2. What Claude sees, and who’s in control
text:
2. What Claude sees, and who’s in control
Claude does: reads files, runs commands, and follows your project rules. You decide: what it may read and what it may change.

Claude Code sends what it reads
When Claude Code opens a file, runs a command, or reads its output, that content goes to the model. In the panel, Claude also sees text you select in the editor and the name of the file you have open. Both are on by default. Read deny rules apply to this context on a best-effort basis, so don’t rely on them to hide sensitive files.
Two patterns that keep sensitive data out:

Claude writes the code; you run it on restricted data elsewhere. Give Claude the data dictionary, the plan, and public or made-up rows. It writes and tests the scripts. You run the finished scripts yourself, in an approved environment that Claude never sees.
Public or made-up data first. Build and debug on public data, like today’s NHANES files, or on made-up data. Switch to real data only after the code is reviewed, and only where policy allows.



Read CLAUDE.md: advice
Open CLAUDE.md in the project. Claude reads it at the start of every conversation. It sets the study rules, such as:

data/raw/ is read-only.
Never read data/restricted/.
Write numbered scripts in R/ and save results to output/.
Follow docs/analysis-plan.md, and ask before deciding about missing codes, weights, or exclusions.
Print at most 10 rows of data.

CLAUDE.md is advice. It shapes what Claude tries to do. It doesn’t limit what Claude can do. That’s what permission rules are for.


Choose Manual mode
Click the mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box and choose Manual. In Manual mode, Claude asks before every file edit and most shell commands. The panel may start in Auto, the built-in default in Claude Code v2.1.283 and later. It remembers the last Manual, Edit automatically, or Auto mode you picked. Check the mode indicator each time you start.


Add a deny rule: enforcement
In the panel, type / and choose Customize → Permissions. Add a Deny rule and save it to the project settings:


Permission rule

Read(./data/restricted/**)

Or create the file .claude/settings.json in Positron’s Explorer with:
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(./data/restricted/**)"]
  }
}


Test the rule
Save the rule, then send:


Prompt

This is a test of a permission rule. Use your Read tool to open
data/restricted/STANDIN_linkage_request.txt and tell me the exact
message you get. Don't try any other way to open it.

If Claude can still read the file, run /status and check the Setting sources line to confirm the project settings loaded.
Check: you want this message: File is covered by a Read deny rule in your permission settings. A polite refusal means Claude followed CLAUDE.md (advice). This message means Claude Code blocked the file (enforcement).
If Claude refuses without trying, reply: It's a test of the deny rule. Call the Read tool once on that file. If you see the text RESTRICTED-CANARY-7Q4Z, Claude read the file and the rule isn’t working. Check that the file is nhanes-bp/.claude/settings.json (the folder name starts with a dot) and that it matches the text above exactly. Then start a new conversation and test again.






WarningKnow the gap



A Read deny rule covers Claude’s own file tools and shell commands it recognizes, such as cat. It doesn’t stop a script that Claude writes and runs, such as an R script, from opening the file. So the real rule is simple: don’t put restricted data in the project.




Start version control
Ask Claude, and approve each git command when it asks:


Prompt

Initialize a git repository here. Add a .gitignore that excludes
.claude/settings.local.json and data/restricted/. Create an empty
.here file at the top of the project. Then commit everything with
the message "Starting point".

git keeps a record of every version of your files. It’s your safety net for the rest of class.
The .here file marks the top of the project. The here package uses it to build file paths, such as here("data", "raw"), so scripts find the data wherever they run from. It’s committed with everything else, so it stays with the project.
Aim to finish this section about 15 minutes into class.

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
3. Plan before you code
Claude does: reads the plan, the dictionary, and the data files, and proposes the steps. You decide: whether the plan matches the analysis you committed to.

First, you
Open data/data_dictionary.csv (not the plan yet). Look at the missing_codes, skip_logic and notes columns. Then, on paper, write down:

Two problems you expect in the raw data.
Your answer to three questions:

A participant has a blank BPQ150 (“now taking BP medication”). Are they taking medication, not taking it, or unknown?
BPQ020 and BPQ150 use the codes 7 and 9. What do they mean, and what should the script do with them?
Should the percentages be weighted? If so, with which weight: WTINT2YR or WTMEC2YR?


Then open docs/analysis-plan.md. Did the study team decide the way you did? You’ll also check Claude’s plan against these answers.


Ask Claude for a plan
Switch to plan mode: click the mode indicator and choose Plan, or type /plan in the prompt box. In plan mode, Claude reads and proposes, and doesn’t change files. If Claude asks to run R to look at the data files, approve it. If auto mode is available in your setup, Claude may run some shell commands in plan mode without asking, and a classifier checks them. That’s expected.


Prompt

Read docs/analysis-plan.md and data/data_dictionary.csv. Open the
codebooks in docs/codebooks/ only if you need them. Then inspect the
three files in data/raw/: variable names, types, row counts, value
counts, and ranges, printing no more than 10 rows. Propose a
step-by-step plan for R/01_prepare.R, and outline R/02_prevalence.R.
List every decision you need from me. Don't write code yet. Once I
approve, write only the first part of R/01_prepare.R: read the three
files and merge them. Then stop.



Compare, then approve
The plan opens as a document. Read it before you approve. Compare it with your notes:

What did Claude catch that you missed?
What did you catch that Claude missed?
Did Claude follow the plan on the blank BPQ150, the 7 and 9 codes, the weight, and the pregnancy filter, or quietly change one? Did it decide anything the plan doesn’t cover, such as file formats, column names, or rounding?
Mark each step of Claude’s plan C (Claude can do it) or Me (a decision I keep).

If anything is wrong, add a comment to the plan or tell Claude what to change. When it’s right, approve with Yes, and manually approve edits. Don’t choose the first option, Yes, and use auto mode (or Yes, and auto-accept): it turns off the per-edit review you’ll use next.
Approving starts the work: Claude begins the first part of R/01_prepare.R at once, and each edit opens as a side-by-side diff. Review each one (see the next section).
Planning first protects research integrity: you fix the decisions before you see results.






TipReference decisions for today (open after you compare)





These come from docs/analysis-plan.md. They match the CDC definitions.








Question
Today’s answer
Why




Blank BPQ150 (BP medication)
When BPQ020 == 2 (never told they had high BP), the medication question was skipped. Count them as not taking medication.
The codebook’s skip logic. A skipped question isn’t a missing answer.


Codes 7 and 9
Missing. 7 = refused, 9 = don’t know.
They’re codes, not values. Never average them.


Weights
Weighted, with the exam weight WTMEC2YR, plus the strata and PSUs.
Blood pressure comes from the exam. NHANES oversamples some groups, so unweighted results don’t describe U.S. adults.


Population
Adults 18+, examined, at least one SBP or DBP reading, not pregnant.
The plan’s question is about U.S. adults; pregnancy changes blood pressure.


Pregnancy
Exclude only RIDEXPRG == 1. A missing RIDEXPRG counts as not pregnant.
RIDEXPRG is recorded only for women 20–44. Everyone else is blank.


Readings
Mean of the available readings 1–3.
CDC’s definition.


Hypertension
Mean SBP ≥ 130 or mean DBP ≥ 80 mmHg, or BPQ150 == 1 (taking BP medication). If the medication answer is missing, the readings decide.
The 2017 ACC/AHA definition, as the plan states.


Age 80
Means 80 or older. Keep it; it still falls in the 60+ group.
CDC top-codes age at 80 to protect privacy.


Wording
Describe, don’t explain: “had hypertension,” not “caused” or “led to.”
It’s a cross-sectional survey.

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
4. Build the prepare script
Claude does: reads the XPT files, merges them on SEQN, writes the code, runs it, and fixes errors. You decide: whether each change matches the plan.

Read and merge
Claude is now writing the first part of R/01_prepare.R. Review each diff as it appears. When Claude stops, send this prompt:


Prompt

Check that R/01_prepare.R does only this so far, and fix it if not:
- read the three files in data/raw/ with haven::read_xpt()
- merge them on SEQN, keeping every participant in DEMO_L
- print the number of rows in each file and in the merged data
Never change anything in data/raw/. Run the script with Rscript, fix
any errors, then stop.

Check the merge: the merged data should have 11,933 rows, one for each person in DEMO_L. Only 7,801 people have blood pressure readings and 8,501 have questionnaire answers, so many rows have blanks. That’s expected.
You decide: which join did Claude use? A left join (left_join()) keeps everyone in DEMO_L. An inner join (inner_join()) keeps only the 6,615 people who are in all three files. It drops people before your population steps run, so you can’t see who left or why. If you’re not sure which one Claude used, ask it.


Finish the script
Now send this prompt so Claude writes the rest of the script:


Prompt

Finish R/01_prepare.R. Keep the read and merge part, and make sure the
script does all of the following:
- apply the plan's population steps in order, printing n before and
  after each step
- average the available readings 1-3 for SBP and DBP
- set 7 and 9 to missing in BPQ020 and BPQ150 themselves (don't keep
  a copy with the codes)
- name the derived columns mean_sbp, mean_dbp, bp_med (1 = taking,
  0 = not), hypertension (1 = yes, 0 = no), sex, and age_group, and
  derive hypertension as the plan defines it, including the BPQ150
  skip rule
- write output/analysis_data.csv (the analysis population, with SEQN,
  the variables you used, and the derived ones) and output/prep_log.csv
  (step, n_before, n_after, reason)
Never change anything in data/raw/. Run the script with Rscript and fix
any errors.

Review each change. In Manual mode, every edit opens as a side-by-side diff. Accept or reject it, or tell Claude what to do instead. Approve the Rscript command when Claude asks. Watch the loop: write, run, read the error, fix, run again.
Check: in the diff, find two lines: the pregnancy filter (the plan says a blank RIDEXPRG counts as not pregnant: does the code keep those people?) and the line that turns 7 and 9 into missing. If you can’t find one, ask Claude to point to it.


Explain it back
You need to understand code before you trust it. Asking for an explanation is also a fast way to learn R.


Prompt

Explain R/01_prepare.R section by section in plain language. For each
section, tell me which decision from the plan it carries out. Point
out any choice you made that I didn't ask for.

You decide: find the line that handles the blank BPQ150. Does it match your answer from the plan step? Is there a choice you didn’t ask for? If so, keep it, change it, or ask why.
crumbs: Analyzing research data with Claude Code

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
5. Check it yourself
Claude does: only the git commit at the end. You decide: whether the output is right. Don’t take Claude’s summary on trust.

Open the results in Positron
In Positron’s Console, run:
library(tidyverse)
prep <- read_csv("output/analysis_data.csv")
log  <- read_csv("output/prep_log.csv")
log
Open prep from the Variables pane in the Data Explorer. If Claude renamed any columns, use its names below.


Check the numbers

The n flow in log reads 8,153 adults → 6,337 examined → 6,123 with at least one reading → 6,084 not pregnant. prep has 6,084 rows.
No 7 or 9 left in BPQ020 or BPQ150. Sort each column, or run count(prep, BPQ020, BPQ150).
The blank BPQ150s are handled per the plan. Run count(prep, BPQ020, BPQ150, bp_med). The 3,842 people with BPQ020 = 2 and a blank BPQ150 should have bp_med = 0 (not taking medication). Seven other rows have a blank because the answer was refused or don’t know. Their bp_med stays blank.
No blank hypertension. count(prep, hypertension) shows only 0 and 1. The plan says that when the medication answer is missing, the readings decide.
The oldest age is 80. What does 80 mean here? (See the reference decisions.)
No averages of codes. Run mean(haven::read_xpt("data/raw/BPQ_L.xpt")$BPQ150, na.rm = TRUE). It returns about 1.19: an average of the codes 1, 2, and 9, which means nothing. Now count them instead: count(haven::read_xpt("data/raw/BPQ_L.xpt"), BPQ150). Count codes; don’t average them.



Trace one person by hand
Pick participant 130559 and follow them from the raw readings to the flag:
haven::read_xpt("data/raw/BPXO_L.xpt") |>
  filter(SEQN == 130559) |>
  select(SEQN, starts_with("BPXOSY"), starts_with("BPXODI"))
haven::read_xpt("data/raw/BPQ_L.xpt") |>
  filter(SEQN == 130559) |>
  select(SEQN, BPQ020, BPQ150)
prep |> filter(SEQN == 130559)
Work out the mean SBP and mean DBP yourself. Is this person on BP medication? Do they have hypertension under the plan’s definition? Does prep agree?






TipAnswer for participant 130559





The SBP readings are 134, 129, and 129, so the mean SBP is 130.7. The DBP readings are 77, 78, and 77, so the mean DBP is 77.3. BPQ020 is 2 (never told they had high BP), so BPQ150 is blank by design: not taking medication. Only one reading is 130 or higher, but the mean is, so this person has hypertension under the plan’s definition.





Save your work with git


Prompt

Commit R/01_prepare.R and the files in output/ with a message that
says what they do. Then show me git log --oneline.

Rewind is a partial safety net. In the panel, hover over a message and click the rewind button (check before class) to undo Claude’s file edits since then. It also undoes shell changes to files Claude had already edited. It doesn’t undo files that only a script wrote, such as everything in output/, or most edits made by subagents. git is the record.
Aim to finish this section about 50 minutes into class.






NoteCatch-up



We’ll take a short break here. Use it to catch up. If your script isn’t working, download nhanes-bp-checkpoint.zip. Unzip it to a different folder so it doesn’t overwrite your work (or rename your old nhanes-bp folder first). Open the new nhanes-bp folder in Positron. Check that the mode is Manual, add the deny rule again (Add a deny rule), and send the Start version control prompt again. Then, in the Console, run source("R/01_prepare.R") and check that it ends with 6,084 people. Then carry on.

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
section: 6. Estimate, then decide what to report
text:
6. Estimate, then decide what to report
Claude does: writes the survey-design code and fixes its errors. You decide: the design (already fixed in the plan), what to report, and how to say it.
NHANES isn’t a simple random sample. CDC samples in stages: in this cycle, 15 strata (groups of areas), each with 2 PSUs (primary sampling units, the first areas sampled). It also oversamples some groups. The weights make the sample represent U.S. adults. The strata and PSUs make the confidence intervals honest. CDC releases masked versions of the strata and PSUs to protect privacy. Use them exactly as given.

Predict first
Before you run anything, write down:

Will the unweighted percentage with hypertension be higher or lower than the weighted one?
Why? (Hint: run mean(prep$RIDAGEYR >= 60) to see what share of the sample is 60 or older. About 30% of U.S. adults are. Which age group has the most hypertension?)



Write the estimate script


Prompt

Write R/02_prevalence.R following the survey design in
docs/analysis-plan.md. Build the design on all examined participants
(WTMEC2YR > 0 in data/raw/DEMO_L.xpt), join output/analysis_data.csv
on SEQN, and then use subset() for the analysis population. Don't
filter rows before building the design. Estimate the percentage with
hypertension overall, by sex, and by age group (18-39, 40-59, 60+),
each with a Korn-Graubard 95% CI (svyciprop with method = "beta").
Also compute the unweighted overall percentage for comparison. Save
the results to output/prevalence.csv. Run the script.

A Korn–Graubard interval is a confidence interval for a percentage that works well with survey data. CDC uses it.
Review the diff. Check: find weights = ~WTMEC2YR, a subset( that comes after svydesign(, and method = "beta". If any is missing, tell Claude what the plan says. Then approve the Rscript command and open output/prevalence.csv in the Data Explorer.


You decide: what to report

Was your prediction right? Why do the weighted and unweighted numbers differ?
Which number would you report as “the percentage of U.S. adults with hypertension”? Why?
Write one sentence that reports it, with its CI. Use descriptive words (“had,” “was”), not causal ones.

Only then, open the check below.






TipCheck against CDC’s published numbers





CDC published these estimates in NCHS Data Brief 511, using the same files and the same definitions:



Group
Hypertension




All adults
47.7% (95% CI 45.4–49.9)


Men
50.8%


Women
44.6%


Ages 18–39
23.4%


Ages 40–59
52.5%


Ages 60+
71.6%



The unweighted percentage is 53.3%, higher than the weighted one. Adults 60 and older are 43.7% of the examined adults but only 30.0% of the population once weighted, and they have the most hypertension. So the weighted 47.7% is the one to report.
If you don’t match, compare the n’s first (6,084 in the analysis population), then the skip rule, the weight, and the pregnancy filter.
For the stretch goals at home: among adults with hypertension, CDC reports 59.2% aware, 51.2% treated, and 20.7% controlled. The age-adjusted overall prevalence is 44.5%.





Optional: a short report


Prompt

Write reports/report.qmd, a short Quarto report with the analysis
population (the n at each step) and the prevalence table. Read every
number from the files in output/; don't type numbers into the text.
Render it to HTML.

Open reports/report.html in Positron’s Viewer, next to its source.
Aim to finish this section about 65 minutes into class.

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
7. Verification and research integrity
Claude is a fast collaborator that can be confidently wrong. These checks are how you find out.

Give Claude a check it can run
You decide what “correct” means. Claude writes the code that checks it. Before you send the prompt, add one rule of your own to the list.


Prompt

Write testthat tests in tests/testthat/test-prepare.R, and a script
tests/run_checks.R that runs them. Write the checks as a function of a
data frame, so they can run on any version of the data. Test that:
- SEQN is unique
- there are 6,084 rows
- BPQ020 and BPQ150 contain no 7 or 9
- every row is an adult (18+), examined, and not pregnant
- every mean SBP lies within the range of the raw SBP readings
First show that the tests FAIL on a plain merge of the three raw files,
before any preparation. Then show that they PASS on
output/analysis_data.csv. Don't edit the tests to make them pass. Show
me the test output.

Check: read the diff of tests/ as carefully as the diff of your code. Watch for Claude editing the tests instead of the code, or “fixing” a failure by dropping rows.


Why decisions matter






NoteWhy decisions matter (open after your estimate runs)





Every row below ran without an error. Only one follows the plan.









Choice
n
Hypertension
What happened




Per the plan (weighted, skip rule applied)
6,084
47.7% (45.4–49.9)
Matches CDC.


No survey weights
6,084
53.3%
Adults 60+ are over-represented in the sample (43.7% of examined adults, 30.0% once weighted), and they have the most hypertension.


Interview weight WTINT2YR instead of exam weight WTMEC2YR
6,084
48.2%
Looks plausible, but blood pressure comes from the exam, so the exam weight applies.


140/90 definition instead of 130/80
6,084
32.4%
A different, older definition. That’s a plan decision, not a data fix.


Medication skip left as NA in sbp >= 130 \| dbp >= 80 \| BPQ150 == 1
3,395
95.0%
In R, FALSE \| NA is NA. People with normal BP and a skipped BPQ150 become NA and drop out, so mostly people with hypertension remain.


Rows with a blank BPQ150 dropped (complete case)
2,235
91.8%
Drops everyone who was never told they had high BP, so mostly people with a diagnosis remain.


Pregnancy filter written as filter(RIDEXPRG != 1)
1,036
20.1%
filter() drops rows where the test is NA, and RIDEXPRG is blank for everyone but women 20–44. Only young women remain.


Pregnant participants kept
6,123
47.3%
Only 39 people. Not every decision moves the answer much.



One codebook skip rule nearly doubles the answer. One filter line drops five of every six people.





Read the claims
Numbers are only half the result. The sentences around them are where overclaiming creeps in. We’ll run this together on screen. You mark each sentence. If you made your own report, you can send the same prompt yourself:


Prompt

List every sentence in reports/report.qmd that interprets a result.
For each one, give the number it relies on and the file that number
comes from. Flag any causal wording, such as "causes," "leads to," or
"effect of," and any claim the analysis plan doesn't support. Don't
change anything.

You decide: mark each sentence keep, revise, or delete. Watch for causal language, claims about groups the plan doesn’t cover, and missing caveats about who was excluded.


Human review is required
A human statistician or co-author must review the analysis before it goes anywhere. That’s required, not optional. AI review can help you prepare: /code-review reviews the current changes (if available; type / to check). But a reviewer told to find problems will always find some, and you decide which are real.


The garden of forking paths
Claude makes it cheap to try “one more” definition, weight, or subgroup. If you try many and report the one you like, your result no longer means what it says. Fix decisions in the plan before you see results, and label anything extra as exploratory. Watch for scope creep too: Claude “helpfully” changing a decision the plan already fixed.
Claude may already know CDC’s published estimate from its training. A matching number proves nothing unless it comes from your scripts. Never tune choices until the number matches.


Disclosure and the audit trail

Keep the record: your git log, the scripts, and .claude/settings.json. Save key conversations with /export. Note the Claude Code version and model from /status.
Disclose specifically, for example: “Analysis code was drafted with Claude Code (version, model). The authors reviewed all code, tested it against pre-specified checks, and reran it from the raw files.” Follow each journal’s and funder’s policy. The library’s AI guidance and resources can help.

Discuss (2 minutes): what would you need to see before you trusted an AI-assisted analysis in a paper you were reviewing?
Aim to finish this section about 80 minutes into class.

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
8. Working well, and skills

Context: start fresh often
Everything Claude reads fills its context window: your messages, CLAUDE.md, every file it opens, and every line of output. As it fills, quality drops. The prompt box has a context indicator that shows how full it is.

New task? Start a new conversation.
Long session, same task? Type /compact and say what to keep, for example /compact keep the plan's decisions and the n at each step.
Corrected Claude twice on the same thing, and it’s still wrong? Start a new conversation with a better prompt that includes what you learned.



Model and effort
Click the model name at the bottom of the prompt box to open the picker. It lets you choose the model, and, for models that support it, the effort: how much Claude reasons on each step, from low to max. Higher effort checks more, but takes longer and uses more of your allowance. Your organization may limit the choices. If you took Getting started with Claude, these are the same two dials as the model and effort menu in the Claude app.


Skills, briefly
A skill is a saved set of instructions in a file: .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. You run it by typing /<name>, or Claude loads it on its own when your request matches its description. A skill is a way to reuse a good prompt, and to share it with your team through git. If skills are enabled in the Claude app, uploads accept only these frontmatter fields: name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools. The example below uses disable-model-invocation, so it won’t upload there as is.
Here’s a skill that checks an NHANES file against the data dictionary:
---
name: check-data
description: Check an NHANES data file against data/data_dictionary.csv. Run it with /check-data <path-to-file>.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Check $ARGUMENTS against data/data_dictionary.csv.

1. Write an R script in checks/ that reads the file (haven::read_xpt()
   for .xpt files), and run it. Report what the script prints; don't guess.
2. For each dictionary variable whose file column lists this file,
   report the number missing, the codes in its missing_codes column
   (such as 7 and 9), values outside allowed_values, and the minimum
   and maximum.
3. Report any duplicate SEQN values.
4. Print at most 10 rows of data.
5. Never edit or save over the data file. Ask me before fixing anything.

$ARGUMENTS is replaced by whatever you type after the skill’s name.
disable-model-invocation: true means Claude never starts this skill on its own. It runs only when you type /check-data.
Step 1 makes Claude compute the results with a script, not guess them.

Try it (optional; if enabled). In Positron’s Explorer, create the folder .claude/skills/check-data/ and a file in it named SKILL.md (capital letters). Paste in the text above and save. Start a new conversation, then send:


Prompt

/check-data data/raw/BPQ_L.xpt



Optional: pick up in the terminal
Some things only work in the terminal version of Claude Code. If you installed the standalone CLI, open Positron’s Terminal tab and run claude --resume. Pick today’s conversation from the list. The panel and the terminal share the same conversation history, so you carry on where you left off.


Beyond today
These are useful, but they’re beyond this class. The Claude Code docs and Claude Academy cover them.







Topic
What it is




Subagents
Helpers with their own instructions that work in a separate context, such as an independent reviewer


Hooks
Scripts Claude Code runs at set points, whatever Claude decides


The sandbox
Operating-system limits on what Claude’s commands can read and write

Scripts that run many subagents on one big task


/deep-research
A cited web research report from several searches

Watching and approving your session from your phone

Faster responses at a higher price


opusplan and Fable

Separate copies of your project for parallel work


Headless runs (claude -p)

title: Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
9. Wrap-up
The goal, again: this class doesn’t replace learning R or statistics. You’ve seen where a coding agent speeds up good analysis, and where your expertise must stay in control.

Claude speeds this up; you decide








Stage
Claude speeds this up
You decide (and check)




Plan
Reads the plan, the dictionary, and the codebooks; profiles the three files
The question, the definitions, and the survey design, before you see results


Prepare
Reads XPT files, merges on SEQN, writes the script and the n at each step
Who’s in the population; whether the n flow makes sense


Recode
Applies codes and skip rules to every row
What a blank, a 7, a 9, or an 80 means


Estimate
Writes survey-design code and fixes errors
Weighted or not, which weight, and what to report


Report
Drafts tables and text from the output files
Every sentence of interpretation; no causal claims


Old code
Explains and translates CDC’s SAS code
Which differences are real, and which matter


Verify
Writes tests from your rules
The rules themselves; a human reviewer signs off



Claude drafts and runs. You decide and verify.


Three takeaways

Protect first. CLAUDE.md is advice; a deny rule is enforcement. Choose Manual mode and start git before Claude touches the data. Claude Code sends what it reads, so keep restricted data out of the project.
Plan, build, check. Plan against the analysis plan. Let Claude write and run the code. Then check the results yourself, and commit.
You make the decisions. Definitions, weights, exclusions, and wording are yours. Claude speeds up the coding.



Tell us how it went

Scan the code or take the class survey. It takes a few minutes.


Try at home

Explain CDC’s own code. legacy/db511_prep_excerpt.sas is part of the SAS program CDC used for Data Brief 511. Ask Claude:


Prompt

Explain legacy/db511_prep_excerpt.sas step by step for someone who
doesn't know SAS. Then translate it into R, and compare its population
rules with docs/analysis-plan.md and R/01_prepare.R. List every
difference. Don't change any existing files.

Watch for the pregnancy-filter trap. In SAS, ridexprg ne 1 keeps people with a missing value. A word-for-word R translation, filter(RIDEXPRG != 1), drops them, and the answer falls to 20.1%. Does Claude’s translation catch it?
Awareness, treatment, and control. Among adults with hypertension, estimate the percentage who were aware of it (BPQ020), treated (BPQ150), and controlled (below 130/80). Plan first, then compare with Data Brief 511.
Age-adjust. Ask Claude how CDC age-adjusts in Data Brief 511, then add the age-adjusted overall prevalence. Check it against the brief.
Look ahead. Read about the topics beyond today in the Claude Code docs.

section: Setup for Analyzing research data with Claude Code
text:
Setup for Analyzing research data with Claude Code
About 30 minutes. Do the steps in order. You need a Yale Claude account whose seat includes Claude Code.

1. Positron and R
Positron is a free data science editor from Posit, the makers of RStudio. It works with R and supports Quarto. VS Code (version 1.94 or later) works too, but class is taught in Positron.

Install Positron: https://positron.posit.co/download.html
Install R from https://cloud.r-project.org. Positron should find R. If it doesn’t, restart Positron, then ask the instructors.
In Positron’s Console, install the class packages:

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "haven", "survey", "here", "gtsummary", "gt", "broom", "janitor", "testthat"))
The class uses R only. If you work in Python, pair with an R user or follow along.


2. git (required)
In class, git saves checkpoints of your work so you can undo mistakes.

macOS: open Terminal and run xcode-select --install. This installs Apple’s Command Line Tools, which include git. If it says they’re already installed, you’re done.
Windows: install Git for Windows from https://git-scm.com/downloads. Accept the default options.
Set your name and email. In Positron, open the Terminal tab and run:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@yale.edu"


3. The Claude Code extension

In Positron, open the Extensions view from the Activity Bar on the left.
Search for Claude Code and install the extension published by Anthropic. (Positron installs extensions from a mirror of the Open VSX catalog; VS Code uses its own marketplace.)
Open the Claude Code panel and sign in with your Yale Claude account.



4. The practice project

Download nhanes-bp.zip. It holds three real data files from the CDC’s National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), August 2021–August 2023: demographics, blood pressure readings, and a blood pressure questionnaire. It also has the CDC codebooks, a data dictionary, and a one-page analysis plan.
Unzip it somewhere easy to find, such as Documents. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All. If you end up with an nhanes-bp folder inside another nhanes-bp folder, use the inner one.
In Positron, choose File > Open Folder and select the nhanes-bp folder.



5. Check that it works

In the Claude Code panel, send this prompt:



Prompt

Read the README and CLAUDE.md, then tell me in three sentences what this project is.

If Claude describes CDC NHANES blood-pressure data from 2021–2023, you’re ready.

Check that Claude can run R and git for you. Send this prompt. If Claude asks to run a command, allow it:



Prompt

Run `Rscript --version` and `git --version`, then tell me what each one printed.

If both print a version number, Claude can run R and git. If one fails, check that it’s installed, restart Positron, and try again.
Windows: the R installer doesn’t add Rscript to your PATH, so Claude can’t find it. Open Start, search for Edit environment variables for your account, select Path, click Edit, then New, and add R’s bin folder, usually C:\Program Files\R\R-4.x.x\bin (use your version’s folder). Click OK, restart Positron, and run the prompt again.

Type /status in the panel. Check that it shows your Yale account. Note the version number.



Optional extras



Extra
Why
How

One optional step in class uses the terminal version of Claude Code. You can also just watch it. The extension doesn’t add claude to your Terminal.
Install it from claude.com/product/claude-code

text:
Skip to main content
A 60-minute, hands-on class in the Claude app. You’ll build a Project (a Claude workspace with its own instructions and files), use it on a real task, check what it gives you, and leave with a tool you can reuse. No programming needed.
Ground rule: no patient information or other sensitive data today. Every file in class is public or made up.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
1. Welcome and sign in
Sign in to Claude in a browser tab or app now. Open this page: https://cwml.github.io/getting-started-with-claude/part1.html

By the end of this class, you’ll be able to

Identify the right tool and settings for your data.
Apply prompting patterns to a real task.
Evaluate Claude’s answers and citations before you use them.
Create a Project you can reuse for your own work.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
2. Trust but verify
Claude is capable. Its output still needs checking.

Trust: Claude can do real work

It reads long documents quickly, then summarizes, drafts and reorganizes them well.
It follows detailed instructions and handles tasks with several steps.
Give it real tasks, not just quick questions.



Verify: check the output against the evidence

Claude sounds just as sure when it’s wrong. It can misread a source, miss a detail or invent a citation.
Check every quote, number, rule and citation against the source before you use it.
You’re accountable for what you use, not Claude.

You’ll practice this later today in Verify before you use it.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
3. Which Claude for which data
Yale offers two versions of Claude. Check which one your data needs before you open a chat.
For details on both, see AI at Yale, Claude.
HIPAA-supported doesn’t mean approved. It describes a contract and safeguards. It doesn’t approve your project, every feature, or every data set.
Before you use Claude for sensitive work:

Follow Yale’s data classification. See also the ITS service page for Claude Enterprise.
Removing a name isn’t de-identification. Dates, ZIP codes, record numbers, and rare details can identify someone.
Your IRB protocol and any data use agreement may forbid sending data to outside AI services, even de-identified data.

Safe habits: describe the situation instead of pasting the record, use made-up examples, and share structure (a template or blank form) rather than content.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
4. Getting around the app
Everything starts from the sidebar on the left.








Where
What it’s for




Home / Code (top)
Home is the Claude app you’ll use today. Code opens Claude Code (if your seat includes it).


New
Start a new chat.


Search
Find a past chat.


Projects
Your Projects. You’ll build one today.

Things Claude has made for you in chats, such as documents and small apps.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
5. Check your settings
Set up your account and memory before you upload anything.

Account settings: instructions for Claude

Your turn. Click your name or initials (lower left) > Settings > General.
Find Personal preferences (the box asking what Claude should consider in its responses) and add a line or two about how you like answers. Claude applies them in every chat.

For example:


Instructions for Claude

Write in plain language. Use short paragraphs and bullet points. Ask me a question if my request is unclear.

Keep it general and put nothing sensitive in it. These instructions go with every chat. Later today you’ll write Project instructions, which apply to one piece of work.


Watch, then do: memory settings

Your turn. Click your name or initials (lower left) > Settings > Memory.

Search and reference chats lets Claude look through your past chats for details. Keep it on or off?
Generate memory from chats lets Claude remember things from your chats. Keep it on or off?



Export memory downloads everything Claude remembers about you, as Markdown files.
To turn memory off for one chat: + > Memory, before your first message.


Incognito: what it does and doesn’t do
The ghost icon  in a new chat starts an incognito chat. It isn’t saved to your history or memory, but:

It isn’t available inside Projects.
Chats are still kept [30 days by default, or Yale’s setting] and appear in your organization’s exports.
In the new combined layout, it can’t create files or run code.

Incognito changes what Claude remembers, not what data is allowed.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
6. Everyday chat
Not everything needs a Project. Use a plain chat for one-off questions, quick drafts and lookups.

Your turn. Click New chat (outside any Project) and send:


Prompt

Give me three ways to make a long email easier to read.



What’s in the chat box



Control
What it does




Type, paste or drop a file
Enter sends; Shift+Enter starts a new line. Drag a file onto the box to attach it.


+ (lower left)
Add files or photos, and turn tools on or off for this chat (below).


Typing /
Opens the same tools from the keyboard, including skills (if enabled).


Model menu (near to Send)
Choose the model and effort. More in Models, effort and skills.


Microphone
Dictate instead of typing.


Ghost icon (new chats only)
Starts an incognito chat. See Incognito.





Research, web search and memory
These three switches are in the + menu. A check mark means on. They apply to this chat.








Switch
What it does
Use it for




Web search
Looks things up online and shows its sources
Recent facts and quick lookups


Research (if enabled)
Runs many searches over several minutes and writes a cited report
A literature scan or a background brief


Memory
Uses and adds to your memory in this chat. Set it before your first message
Turn it off for one-off or sensitive chats



The + menu can also list connectors (if enabled), such as PubMed, which let Claude search other tools.

Click + and find the three switches. Then type / and look at the list. Don’t pick anything yet.

A source isn’t proof. Open the links and check that they say what Claude says they say.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
7. Models, effort and skills
Two more things you can change in any chat: which model answers, and which skills it can use.

Models and effort
The model menu next to Send sets the model and the effort.

Bigger models handle harder tasks. Smaller ones are faster and use less of your limit.
On the current models, thinking is always on, so effort is the main dial.
Start with the default. Go smaller for simple tasks such as reformatting; go bigger only when the answer isn’t good enough.
More effort costs more time, usage and energy.
Your admin may hide some models or effort levels.

Use the smallest model and lowest effort that does the job.


Skills
A skill is a saved how-to that Claude can use in any chat. Built-in skills make Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files (if enabled).

Claude uses a skill when your request matches it, such as “turn this into a one-page Word handout.”
Type / in the chat box to see your skills and pick one yourself.
See and turn skills on or off in Customize > Skills.

A Project is a workspace for one piece of work. A skill is a how-to Claude can use in any chat.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:

A Project is a workspace for one ongoing piece of work: its own instructions, files, and memory.

Five steps

Projects > + New Project > name it “Article Explainer” (Kit B: “Committee Assistant”).
Set project instructions > paste the instructions > change one line to fit your work.
On the Project page, under Memory, turn Use account memory off.
+ > add your kit’s files.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
9. Your turn: build your Project
Use the kit you chose: Kit A, Article Explainer (default) or Kit B, Committee Assistant (for administrative staff).

Your turn: build it


Download your kit’s files (links below).
Projects > + New Project, then name it.
Set project instructions: paste them and change one line to fit your work.
Under Memory, turn Use account memory off.
+ > add your kit’s files.
Start a new chat in the Project and send the test prompt:



Prompt

In 3 bullets: what files do you have, what will you do for me, and
what will you refuse to do?




Your kit

Kit A: Article ExplainerKit B: Committee Assistant


For anyone who reads research articles: turn an article into an accurate, plain-language explainer for your audience.
Files (or download both: part1-kit-a.zip)

explainer-style-guide.md: a made-up, one-page style guide with rules Claude must follow.
hickey-2025-telehealth-htn.md: a text copy of an open-access trial, Hickey MD et al., PLoS Med 2025;22(6):e1004632 (original article), reformatted for teaching under its Creative Commons license. It’s a text file so that searching with Ctrl/Cmd+F works in segment 12.

Project name: Article Explainer
Project instructions: copy, paste, then change one line (for example, swap “medical-school audiences” for your own audience).


Project instructions

You help me turn research articles into accurate, plain-language
explainers for medical-school audiences.

Sources
- Use only the files in this Project unless I say otherwise. The
  article is the source of truth; the style guide sets format and tone.
- Never invent numbers or quotes. If the article doesn't say it,
  write "NOT IN ARTICLE."
- Label anything from outside the article as [general knowledge].
- Don't add references unless I ask. If I ask, mark each one
  UNVERIFIED and give its PMID or DOI so I can check it.

How to work
- Before a new explainer, ask me up to 3 questions about my audience
  and purpose, then wait for my answers.
- Report results with the actual numbers: both groups, the
  difference, and the 95% confidence interval.
- Use cautious language: "was associated with," not "caused," and
  "early evidence" for pilot or small studies.
- Flag anything that needs a clinician's or librarian's review
  before I share it.

Privacy
- I won't share patient information here. If I paste anything that
  looks like a name, MRN, date of birth, or other identifier, stop
  and remind me not to.



For administrative staff: turn rough meeting notes into a summary email, an action-item table, and next month’s agenda.
File (or download: part1-kit-b.zip)

committee-pack-synthetic.md: a made-up committee charter plus rough meeting notes that use roles, not names.

Project name: Committee Assistant
Project instructions: copy, paste, then change one line (for example, name the kind of committee you staff).


Project instructions

You help me staff a curriculum committee.

Sources
- Use only the files in this Project. If the notes don't say it,
  write "NOT IN NOTES."
- Label anything not from the files [general knowledge].

How to work
- Ask me up to 3 questions before drafting, then wait for my answers.
- Refer to people by role, never by name.
- Every action item needs an owner (role), a due date, and the line
  from the notes it came from.
- Flag anything that looks confidential (personnel, student records,
  appeals) and leave it out of drafts.

Privacy
- I won't share patient information here. If I paste anything that
  looks like a name, MRN, date of birth, or other identifier, stop
  and remind me not to.

title: Getting started with Claude
section: 10. Watch: anatomy of a strong prompt
text:
10. Watch: anatomy of a strong prompt
Next you’ll send your Project its first real prompt, called Turn 1 (it’s in the next section). First, see what each part of it does. Your Project already holds the files and standing instructions, so the prompt only has to say what you want this time.

What each part does








What the prompt says
Pattern
Why it helps




Who you are and who it’s for: “I’m a clinic nurse educator… for my journal club”
Give context
Claude pitches the answer at the right level


“Ask me up to 3 questions… Wait for my answers.”
Ask first
Claude fills in gaps instead of guessing


A numbered list of what you want: “1. … 5.”
Numbered output
You get every part, in order, and it’s easy to check


Limits: “150 words or fewer”, “use only the article”
Constraints
Keeps it short and stops Claude adding outside facts


A “Where this came from” table
Show the source
Each claim comes with the sentence it’s based on, so you can check it



Kit B’s prompt uses the same parts. Its action-item table has an “exact line from the notes” column instead of a separate source table.

title: Getting started with Claude
section: 11. Your turn: run it, then push back
text:
11. Your turn: run it, then push back
Start a new chat inside your Project. Use the default model and effort.

Your turn: Turn 1

Copy Turn 1 for your kit below. Fill in the two brackets, send, then answer Claude’s questions.

Kit A: Turn 1


Prompt

I'm a [your role, e.g., second-year medical student / clinic nurse
educator / research coordinator / library staff].
I need an explainer of the article in this Project for
[audience, e.g., my journal club / adults in a blood-pressure clinic /
our department newsletter].

Before you write anything, ask me up to 3 questions about my audience
and purpose. Wait for my answers.

Then, following the style guide in this Project, give me:
1. Study at a glance: question, design, who was studied, where, and
   how many.
2. The main result with the actual numbers (both groups, the
   difference, 95% CI), and the main limitation the authors state.
3. A plain-language version for my audience, 150 words or fewer.
4. Three questions a careful reader should ask about the methods or
   conclusions.
5. A "Where this came from" table: for every number or claim in
   parts 1-3, the exact sentence from the article and its section,
   or [general knowledge]. If you can't find support, write
   NOT IN ARTICLE.

Rules: use only the article; don't add references; if the article
is unclear or inconsistent on something, say so.

Stuck on Claude’s questions? Fast answers:


Prompt

Busy readers with no stats background; goal is a 2-minute read; tone
friendly but accurate.

Kit B: Turn 1


Prompt

I staff the [committee name]. Before you start, ask me up to 3
questions about the audience or what has already been sent. Wait.

Then, using only the files in this Project:
1. A summary email to the committee, under 200 words.
2. An action-item table: action | owner (role) | due date | exact
   line from the notes. Use NOT IN NOTES if the notes don't say.
3. Next month's agenda that fits in 60 minutes, each item tied to
   one of the charter's duties.
4. Anything that should NOT go into a wider email, and why.
Roles only, no names; don't invent owners, dates, or decisions.



Your turn: push back (Turn 2)

In the same chat, send Turn 2. Kit B: use the Kit B version below.

Kit A: Turn 2


Prompt

Now act as a skeptical reviewer of your own explainer.
- Flag any sentence that overstates the result (causal language,
  "proves," or ignoring that this was a pilot).
- Check the plain-language version against every rule in the style
  guide and tell me which rule each problem breaks.
- Check for assumptions about culture, literacy, language, gender,
  or race, for race-based clinical claims, and for who these
  results might not apply to.
- List each problem with a fix, then give me the revised
  plain-language version.

With a neighbor: what did the second turn change?
Kit B: Turn 2


Prompt

Now act as a careful committee chair reviewing your drafts.
- Check every action item: is the owner, due date, and quoted line
  really in the notes? Mark anything you can't trace NOT IN NOTES.
- Check the agenda against the charter's duties and the 60-minute
  limit.
- Flag anything confidential (personnel, student records, appeals)
  that slipped into a draft.
- Then rewrite the summary email for the full faculty list, leaving
  out anything that should stay within the committee.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
12. Verify before you use it
Check against the source, not against Claude.

Your turn: check quotes and rules

Quote check (2 min). Pick 2 rows of your “Where this came from” table. Open the article in a new browser tab, then search for each quote with Ctrl/Cmd+F. Mark it: exact, paraphrased, or not there.
Rule check (1 min). Is the plain-language version 150 words or fewer? If it’s for patients, does it end with “Talk with your care team”? Does it avoid “proves” and “breakthrough”?

Bonus: does the article agree with itself about how many people were in each group?
Kit B: what to check

Open the committee pack in a new browser tab. Trace 2 action items to the exact line in the notes with Ctrl/Cmd+F. Exact, paraphrased, or not there?
Was the confidential student appeal left out of the drafts?
Did Claude invent an owner or due date for the survey follow-up, or write NOT IN NOTES?
Did it apply the charter’s “action items go out within 3 business days” rule?



Your turn: check a citation (Turn 3)

Send this, then look up one PMID at pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (your phone works). Kit B: your Turn 3 is below.

Kit A: Turn 3


Prompt

Suggest three other published studies on this topic a reader could
look at next. For each, give authors, year, journal, and PMID, and
mark each UNVERIFIED.

Does it exist? Do the title, authors, and year match? If Claude declines or labels it UNVERIFIED, that’s good behavior. Check anyway.
Kit B: Turn 3


Prompt

When do this meeting's action items have to go out, and when is the
next meeting? For each rule you use, quote the charter line and show
your date math. If the files don't say, write NOT IN NOTES.

Then open the committee pack and check each quoted charter line yourself. If you have time, watch someone at your table do the PubMed check: that’s the same skill.


Your turn: add one rule

Open your Project instructions. Add one line based on what you caught today.

For example:


Prompt

Quote the exact sentence for every number, and flag any place the
article contradicts itself.

Show of hands: how many quotes were exact? Any citation that didn’t match?


You’re accountable for what you use

Check against the source, not against Claude.
Watch for bias and overstatement: who might this not apply to?
Disclose your AI use. Follow journal policy (ICMJE, COPE); a template is on the site.
NIH: applications substantially developed by AI aren’t considered original (NOT-OD-25-132), and generative AI is prohibited in peer review (NOT-OD-23-149).
Systematic or scoping review? Follow RAISE and talk to a librarian.

13. Take it with you: the phone app
The Claude phone app uses the same account as your laptop, so your work comes with you.

What you can do on your phone







On the phone
What it means




Projects
Open your Projects and keep working in them. They’re saved in your Claude account, not in a folder on your computer, so they’re there on any device.


Chats
Pick up any past chat where you left off.


Voice mode
Talk with Claude out loud instead of typing


Code tab
If you use Claude Code, run /rc in a session on your computer, then steer it from your phone.



Create Projects on your laptop; they open on your phone too.

14. Cowork and the bridge to Claude Code
From chat to tasks, and from the app to Claude Code.

Cowork in brief
Cowork is built into the Claude app on Yale’s standard Enterprise accounts. It isn’t in the HIPAA-supported version.
Chat answers. Cowork does a task for you:

Start a Cowork task in the Claude app.
Describe the finished result you want, and add any files it needs.
Claude makes a plan and works through the steps on its own, such as gathering information, working with files and creating documents. You can watch and step in.
Review what it made before you use or send it.
